title: Algebraic Data Types & Exhaustive Matching
summary: Sum types and product types as a type-system feature, and compiler-checked exhaustiveness — how to make illegal states literally unrepresentable instead of merely unlikely.

slides.markdown:
The previous Topic's `Option<T>` — a value that's either present or absent, exactly two cases — turns out to be the simplest possible instance of a much more general idea: a type that's *exactly one of several named alternatives*, each possibly carrying its own data. That general idea is a **sum type**, and it's one half of **algebraic data types** (ADTs) — the other half, **product types**, is just structs and tuples under a formal name you already know.

The payoff of naming this formally: once a value's type is a closed set of alternatives, a compiler can check that you've handled *every* alternative — **exhaustiveness checking** — catching a missed case at compile time instead of at whatever moment in production first exercises the case nobody wrote a branch for.

This Topic covers ADTs as a type-system feature — the type-theoretic classification and the exhaustiveness guarantee. Idiomatic map/fold/pattern-matching *usage* of ADTs in day-to-day functional code lives in the `functional` group.

slides.subTitle: "AND" combinations of values
slides.markdown:
A **product type** combines several values into one, all present *simultaneously* — a struct, a record, a tuple. `struct Point { x: Int, y: Int }` is a product type because a `Point` value is an `x` *and* a `y`, both always present together; there's no `Point` that has only one of them.

The name "product" comes directly from counting how many distinct values the type can hold: if `x` can be any of 4 values and `y` can be any of 3 values, `Point` has exactly 4 × 3 = 12 possible values — the count *multiplies*, the way a mathematical product does, because every combination of the two fields' values is a distinct, valid `Point`.

This is the type you already use constantly without the formal name — every class with more than one field, every tuple, every row in a table schema is a product type in this precise sense. Naming it formally matters specifically because it sets up the contrast with sum types next, and "AND-combination, count multiplies" is the exact property that flips for a sum type.

slides.subTitle: "OR" — exactly one of several shapes
slides.markdown:
A **sum type** is the opposite structure: a value is *exactly one* of several named alternatives, never more than one, and different alternatives can carry entirely different data. `enum Shape { Circle(radius: Float), Rectangle(width: Float, height: Float) }` — a `Shape` value is a `Circle` *or* a `Rectangle`, never both, and each alternative carries only the data relevant to *that* shape (a `Circle` has no `width` field to be wrong about, because the type itself excludes it).

The name "sum" again comes from counting values: if `Circle` has as many possible values as there are floats, and `Rectangle` has as many possible values as there are (width, height) pairs, `Shape`'s total possible values is those two counts *added* — every `Shape` value belongs to exactly one alternative's count, with no overlap, unlike a product type's multiplied count where every combination across fields is valid.

This is the generalization `Option<T>`'s "present or absent" was a special case of: `Option<T> = Some(T) | None` is a sum type with exactly two alternatives, one carrying a `T` and one carrying nothing at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Result<T, E> as a box holding either shape
slides.markdown:
`Result<T, E>` — the standard "this operation either succeeds with a `T` or fails with an `E`" sum type used throughout Rust, and as a pattern elsewhere — is the clearest concrete picture of a sum type's actual shape at runtime.

A `Result<T, E>` value is, underneath, one tagged box: a small marker indicating *which* alternative this particular value is (`Ok` or `Err`), plus the payload for that specific alternative and nothing else. An `Ok(value)` box contains its `T` and has no `E`-shaped slot sitting around unused; an `Err(error)` box contains its `E` and has no leftover `T` slot. There is no third state, no way to be both, and no way to be neither — the type itself rules those possibilities out entirely, rather than relying on the programmer to never construct them.

This is the exact structural contrast with a product type: a `Result` isn't "a `T` and an `E`, one of which happens to be unset" (that would be a product type with an unused field, and unused-but-present fields are exactly the illegal-state risk covered later in this Topic) — it's a genuinely single-shaped box whose shape depends on which alternative it is.

slides.sectionTitle: Pattern matching over a sum type

slides.subTitle: Catching missed branches at compile time
slides.markdown:
Because a sum type declares a *closed*, complete list of alternatives — `Shape` is only ever `Circle` or `Rectangle`, nothing else can exist — the compiler can verify, purely by reading the type declaration, whether a `match` handles every single one. Add a new variant to `Shape`, say `Triangle { base: f64, height: f64 }`, without updating the `area` function's `match`, and the compiler rejects the program: "non-exhaustive match, missing pattern: Triangle."

This is fundamentally different from a `switch` statement over, say, an integer or a string in most mainstream languages — an `int`'s set of possible values isn't a closed, enumerable list the compiler could exhaustively check against, so a missing `case` is either silently ignored or requires an explicit `default` you have to remember to add and keep correct. A sum type's closed alternative set is exactly what makes exhaustiveness checking *possible* at all — you cannot get this guarantee from an open-ended type, only from one that declares its complete set of shapes up front.

The practical payoff: adding a new case to a sum type turns every place that needs updating into a compile error, for free, rather than a silent gap you find out about only when that new case actually occurs at runtime.

The deepest practical payoff of sum types is a design technique: instead of representing "which state am I in" with a bag of nullable/boolean fields that *should* only appear in certain combinations, encode the states as a sum type so the combinations that shouldn't exist genuinely **cannot be constructed** — not merely discouraged by a comment or a runtime assertion.

Take a network request's status, modeled the common but weak way: `class RequestState { boolean isLoading; String data; String error; }`. Nothing in this type prevents `isLoading = true` *and* `data` populated *and* `error` populated all at once — a state that makes no sense, but that the type happily allows you to construct, requiring every piece of code that reads a `RequestState` to defensively re-check which combination it actually got.

Remodeled as a sum type — `enum RequestState { Loading, Success(data: String), Failure(error: String) }` — that nonsensical combination simply has no constructor that could produce it. There's no `Success`-and-`Failure`-at-once value, because the type only ever holds exactly one alternative's data. The illegal state didn't become less likely through careful discipline — it became impossible to express in the type system at all, which is a fundamentally stronger guarantee.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: simulating sum types with flags
slides.markdown:
The `RequestState` example in the previous Subtopic is common enough to be worth naming as its own anti-pattern: a struct with several nullable fields and/or boolean flags that are meant to be mutually exclusive, but where the *type* enforces no such exclusivity — only a convention, a comment, or a runtime assertion does.

The concrete cost isn't hypothetical. Every function that consumes a `RequestState`-shaped struct has to defensively re-derive "which logical state is this actually in" from the flag/field combination, and different functions can derive it inconsistently — one function might check `isLoading` first, another might check `error != null` first, and if a caller ever produces a state that violates the intended exclusivity (a bug, a race condition setting two flags), those two functions can disagree about what state the value represents, with no compiler error anywhere flagging the disagreement.

The fix is exactly the previous Subtopic's technique: whenever you notice a set of fields that are meant to appear only in specific combinations, or a boolean whose meaning depends on another field's value, that's the signal to remodel as a sum type — one alternative per legal combination — so the illegal combinations stop being possible to construct rather than merely being possible-but-discouraged.

This Topic has deliberately stayed at the type-theoretic and type-system level: what sum and product types *are*, why exhaustiveness checking is possible for one but not the other, and the illegal-states-unrepresentable design technique they enable. That's the part every statically typed language with ADT support shares.

What this Topic hasn't covered: the idiomatic *functional programming* usage patterns built on top of ADTs — folding over a sum type generically, mapping a transformation across whichever alternative is present without writing an explicit match each time, or treating `Option`/`Result` as instances of a more general "container you can map over" abstraction (a functor, in the vocabulary that group uses). That usage-level material lives in the `functional` group, which assumes this Topic's type-theoretic foundation and builds the day-to-day functional-programming idioms on top of it.

The boundary is deliberate: here, ADTs are a type-system feature you'd recognize in Rust, Kotlin, TypeScript, or Swift regardless of how functionally-styled the surrounding code is; the `functional` group's material is specifically about writing *functional* code that happens to use ADTs as its data model.

"Redesign this state-as-booleans struct so invalid combinations can't compile" is this Topic's standard prompt, and a strong answer moves through three explicit steps rather than jumping straight to a rewritten type.

**First, enumerate the actual legal states** by reading the existing code's usage, not just the field list — for a `RequestState { isLoading, data, error }`, the legal states are probably exactly three: loading (no data, no error), success (data, no error, not loading), failure (error, no data, not loading) — everything else is either currently-impossible-in-practice or an actual latent bug nobody noticed.

**Second, make each legal state one sum-type alternative**, carrying exactly the data that state needs: `enum RequestState { Loading, Success(data: String), Failure(error: String) }` — no alternative has a spare field for data it shouldn't have.

**Third, update every consumer to pattern-match exhaustively**, and treat every compile error this produces as a genuine finding — a consumer that doesn't compile against the new type was making an assumption about the old flag combinations that the redesign has now surfaced explicitly, which is usually where an actual latent bug gets found.

Naming that third step — the compile errors as a feature, not just friction — is what shows you understand why this redesign is valuable, not just how to perform it.

This Topic closes the `type-systems` group by generalizing a thread that ran through several of its Topics: `Option<T>` (null safety) is a two-alternative sum type; a `match`/pattern-match that must handle every alternative connects directly back to dynamic dispatch's "every implementer must handle a message" from the `paradigms` group, but checked statically and exhaustively instead of relying on every implementer existing.

Across this whole group, the throughline has been the same: a static type checker can express and enforce properties about your program's data — when it's checked, how strictly, what shapes it can infer, how generic containers substitute, whether shape or declared name matters, whether absence is tracked, and now, whether a value's alternatives are a closed, exhaustively-checkable set. Each Topic added one more thing a sufficiently expressive type system can catch before your program ever runs — which is the entire practical case for caring about type systems at all, beyond syntax trivia.
